items.title: The Real Selling Point of Romantasy
items.summary: This is an edition of the Books Briefing, our editors’ weekly guide to the best in books. Sign up for it here. Romantasy—the category of fiction in which the supernaturally gifted soar on the wings of love, and also sometimes of dragons—is incredibly successful. Its reigning queen, Sarah J. Maas, has sold about 75 million copies of her novels, my colleague Honor Jones reported in a recent Atlantic essay . The appeal of the genre, Jones found, isn’t just chiseled abs, smoldering gazes, and faerie frippery. Yes, there are hyper-athletic magical trysts, but “far more significant are feelings and friendships between the heroes: enchanted beings with relatable self-esteem issues who don’t just seek and fight but also yearn and banter as they face down enemies,” Jones writes. Readers stay for engaging and emotionally effective stories featuring characters they love. First, here are four new stories from The Atlantic ’s Books section: Good villains are hard to come by. This one’s great. The journalist and the manipulator Immigration is a poorly oiled machine. The man who wanted to understand every aspect of Jewish life Romantasy fans generally know that books like those in Maas’s mega-best-selling A Court of Thorns and Roses series—popularly known by the acronym ACOTAR —aren’t going to win the Pulitzer Prize. And they know that fantasy isn’t real life. “But if they’re snowed in—­or trapped by a pandemic, or up with a nursing newborn, or stuck in any of the ways humans tend to get stuck—­it can help to imagine” the possibility of magic, Jones writes. This reading experience doesn’t require the emotional tumult of picturing oneself in, say, Oliver Twist’s tiny 19th-century orphan shoes—or, more challenging, Fagin’s villainous boots. Instead, ACOTAR and its ilk make imagining easy: You may not know what it’s like to kiss a shape-shifter, but it’s exciting—seductive, even—to picture giving in to an attraction tinged with intrigue and mystery. And doing so is not necessarily less fulfilling than reading literary fare, because practicing this kind of creativity is good for us. It makes life’s hardships more bearable, as Jones indicates, and it also makes reality more interesting. If all we did was describe the mundane to one another, it would be difficult for any of us to have the kind of life worth writing stories about. Every queen-bee genre has its haters. Jones notes that plenty of people in the literary world “lament that the only books that sell now are faerie or dragon or elfpunk porn.” But a better approach would be to learn from romantasy’s success: We sometimes need a reminder that reading can simply be entertaining. And if entertainment comes from imagining what it might be like to have a hunky elf-king hanging around, well, where’s the harm in that? Illustration by Natalie Shields Those Books of Smut and Wonder By Honor Jones How Sarah J. Maas became the queen of romantasy Read the full article. What to Read The Fox Wife , by Yangsze Choo Choo’s novel, set in Manchuria in 1908, blends folklore and classic detective fiction, and adds a dash of fantasy—half of its characters are shape-shifting spirits who transform from foxes to humans and back again. These creatures are as clever and crafty as you might expect, and the narrative twists keep the reader in a state of high alert. What starts as a police procedural about the death of a high-class courtesan soon blossoms into a fantastical quest to break curses, rekindle lost love, and catch a murderer. Although it’s not overly long, the book has a mythic feeling, moving through time and space like an epic poem. Choo seamlessly combines narrative momentum and lush world-building, so the reader discovers the setting and uncovers the mystery alongside the novel’s endearing detective. — M. L. Rio From our list: Eight plot-heavy books that will keep you turning pages Out Next Week 📚 Redemption: Faith, Justice, and Sisterhood on Death Row , by Lawrence Wright 📚 Crooked Cross , by Sally Carson 📚 I Only Shout So You Can Hear Me , by Lil Jon with Paul Cantor Your Weekend Read Illustration by The Atlantic . Source: Gary Gershoff / Getty. Megyn Kelly’s Extreme Makeover By Sophie Gilbert Do you remember Megyn Kelly? I once walked past her in a Chicago O’Hare bathroom in 2016, shortly after Donald Trump had won his first presidential election, and was momentarily stopped in my tracks by both her nuclear-grade charisma and her pixie cut. For a woman to have short hair on Fox News, where Kelly was a star anchor at the time, seemed as seditious to the network’s established order as reading Judith Butler or Karl Marx live on air. But this was a moment during which Kelly seemed to be leaning into the role of crusader for women—speaking out about being sexually harassed by the former Fox News CEO Roger Ailes and so inflaming Trump with her rigorous questioning during one debate that he later insinuated on CNN that she must have had her period. items.title: 15 Small Press Titles You Should Be Reading This Fall
items.summary: Something I have been thinking about a lot—and talking to other industry peers with—is what has happened to media, and specifically books coverage. This is why even if you have just five dollars, you should consider donating to Electric Literature, who is one of the few remaining outlets specifically devoted to literature. Many of the books on this list reflect that same ethos: doing the work when it seems like the larger world might not care. From Ellen O’Connell Whittet’s harrowing novel of a pregnancy journey to Erica Kent’s haunting novel of addiction, or even Drew Buxton’s protagonist Teddy trying to make it as a strongman, the thread running through many of these books is people—or in the case of Open the Floodgates , a sentient river—who keep trying. They keep trying when the odds are against them; they keep trying when there is refugee-camp-level disaster as in Yñiga , Salt in the Snow , and Those Who Vanish ; they keep trying when it’s family disasters, like a teen boy finding his caretaker aunt dead on the floor in The Vivaldi Church or Katherine in Morocco being disinherited for loving the wrong kind of man. People keep going on, and small presses keep offering space for these stories. Dzanc Books: Book of Hours by Ellen O’Connell Whittet Book of Hours follows parts of the protagonist’s life, from childhood through fertility treatment and becoming a mother. The unnamed narrator had visions of saints when she was a girl in Catholic school, and as she experiences her changing body during pregnancies, the visions return. All the while, she is translating a medieval French poem about a miraculous birth, and looking for answers in the text. The novel takes on both the beauty and violence of giving birth alongside the challenges and heartbreak that led up to the protagonist delivering her own child. Whittet has created a novel that allows readers to experience the sacred, both in the religious meaning of the word and the biological inference when new life arrives in the world. Singular. SFWP: Black Dog by Erica Kent Eleven-year-old Jessica Ryder is a smart kid, excels in her English classes, and she has a promising friendship with a neighborhood kid, Dean, as well as a strong pull toward Dean’s chaotic younger brother. When she learns John Lennon has been shot, she’s rocked by the news, and her mostly functional alcoholic father offers what he knows will help: a beer. Jess spirals into addiction while trying to maintain friendships and her relationship to her parents. Set between 1980 and 1989 and marked with historical moments of Gen X childhood, Kent captures both a formative time for a generation alongside Jess’ personal disasters and triumphs. Redemptive and readable. Catalyst Press: Salt in the Snow by Sahra Noor After the death of her mother, a young Sahra Noor has already experienced an incalculable grief when the seeds of the ongoing Somali civil war are planted. She and her family are driven first from Mogadishu and then into a refugee camp. It is in the camp that Sahra takes the first steps in what will become a successful career in public health, but she has a long road to get there. When her immediate family is finally relocated to Minneapolis in the mid-90s, Sahra finds herself on a journey that will test her even harder than fleeing political violence. Riveting. Forest Avenue Press: The Sea-Glass Shore by Julie Salmon Kelleher Rona and Jack are raising their twin son and daughter along a cove in the Pacific Northwest and wrestling with all of the concerns of parenting. Rona—and thus her children—are selkies, or, shapeshifters who can transform from seal to human and back by donning or doffing their sealskin. Living mostly on land in the house Jack built, Rona has a complicated relationship to how her human life has changed her and influenced her children. The Sea-Glass Shore explores cycles of family dynamics, intergenerational conflict, our relationship to the natural world, and ideas of possession and agency from multiple perspectives. Kelleher makes the mythical relatable, as you don’t have to be a selkie to sometimes wonder if you’re in the wrong skin. A charming novel. Melville House: Morocco by Norah Labiner The unnamed narrator of Morocco is an observer who is always at a bit of a distance. This suits her well as a summer intern reader for a horror-focused literary magazine. Concurrently, her friendship with Katherine, an heiress who is the daughter of a renowned psychoanalyst, begins to resemble the same gothic qualities as the stories she’s picked from the slush pile. As the narrator and Katherine move out of their teen years and to adulthood, Katherine’s engagement to a man her father finds unsuitable becomes central. Morocco looks back on a friendship and examines the fallibility of memory. It is immersive and richly textured, deftly layered with literary allusions, and Labiner has written it with exceptional style. Hub City Press: Daytona Teddy Riggs by Drew Buxton It’s 1996, and Teddy Riggs, known as “Daytona” by his friends, is a Corpus Christie high school football star—but high school is over and Daytona is unemployed, on the outs with his parents, living with his elderly grandmother, and consuming an unholy amount of Whataburger on the daily. His dream is to compete in a strong man competition he’s training for, but Buxton’s sardonic novel is about more than a (mostly) loveable meathead: It’s about the intersection of masculinity and vulnerability, power-lifting and powerful social dynamics. Daytona is far from perfect, but his heart is (mostly) as big as his home state of Texas, and it’s easy to root for him. Reverberation Books: Open the Floodgates by Nina Schuyler In a small California town that is grappling with a changing climate and the fallout of prioritizing industry over conservation, Judge Larry Skolnik presides over a courtroom where the plaintiff is the town river. In this imaginative work, The River has been granted the legal right to personhood and is determined to use it. At the same, Skolnik and the other residents of the town find themselves with opposing feelings about what The River deserves, and as they debate outside of the courtroom, fissures in their relationship begin to crack open. Open the Floodgates is a thoughtful and nuanced novel of speculative climate fiction layered with messy human relationships and an overtone of dire environmental consequences. Arte Público Press: They Hold Grudges by Diana Rojas The Costa Rican diaspora where Rob lives in Rhode Island is composed mostly of his family, but they are close—Rob and his wife, for example, live on the same block as his parents—and the family loves chisme, or to gossip. Yet when Rob dreams of a terrible crime allegedly committed by his cousin, and his sister has corroborating dreams, the chisme begins to spiral, and Rob is accused of his own terrible crime. He wants to clear his name, but having grown up with his Abuelito’s story of his warring brothers, he also wants to maintain family harmony. In They Hold Grudges , Diana Rojas picks at the threads that weave a close-knit family together, exploring how families negotiate and test loyalties, growing either closer together or farther apart in the process. Complicated and compelling. Nightboat Books: Tricyclist by Joon Oluchi Lee It’s the early aughts in San Francisco, and Howie Song is a ballet dancer who has consistent work in a dance company but no starring roles, and his cadre of lesbian friends are welcoming but sometimes leave him wondering. Through a series of nights out, a funeral for a cat, and Howie’s own distance to his emotional life, Tricyclist has Howie often positioned as a third wheel. Yet, while Howie is emotionally ambivalent, with lovers and hookups he is physically present: His rich sexual life, often described in refreshingly non-euphemistic detail, is a kind of anchor; it is also a reclamation of a past partner who weaponized intimacy. items.title: 10 Books Exploring Estrangement as the Only Route for Survival
items.summary: At the age of 18, I ran away from the rural South and cut contact with my entire family. I fled halfway across the country and began college as a first generation, low income college student. I legally changed my name, found solace in writing, and grafted roots through my chosen family. I will never reconcile with my ex-family. Yet, I have been told by survivors and non-estranged people over and over that I would never heal if I didn’t forgive my abusive parents. I believe that forgiveness isn’t essential in my healing journey; escape was. Approximately a quarter of Americans are estranged from at least one relative , yet the topic of cutting ties remains largely taboo. Oprah released two episodes addressing estrangement as a trend, despite exiters and experts identifying how calling it a trend is dangerous. When healthy relationships are missing from one’s family, the ticket for safety may be through estrangement. After leaving an abusive relationship (whether familial or otherwise) establishing agency is one of the most healing acts. As someone who has been estranged from her entire family for 13 years, I longed for narratives that mirrored my own: that it was possible to flee family and build a better life away from abuse. As social discourse surrounding estrangement has become inflamed, my hope is that our narratives reduce the stigma of family estrangement. I’m sick of how child abuse victims are silenced or told repeatedly to forgive and reconcile with harmful parents. My life’s mission is to destigmatize those of us who choose safety over family. Estrangement is a spectrum. It can arise from one or many reasons, such as abuse, religion, addiction, mental illness, politics, as well as forced separation due to war and other human rights violations. While many estranged relationships hover around low contact or cordial contact, I am interested in child abuse survivors who—like me—found solace in complete estrangement. These 10 books explore what happens when survival is only possible through estrangement. What My Bones Know by Stephanie Foo Journalist and radio producer Stephanie Foo, in her debut and New York Times bestselling memoir, utilizes a braided narrative to explore her experience surviving childhood abuse alongside investigative reporting on Complex-Post Traumatic Stress Disorder (cPTSD). Foo interweaves personal narrative alongside transcripts from therapy, interviews with psychologists, in-depth visualizations during EMDR, and anecdotes of hope to portray the mental health impact of familial abuse. Foo grapples with a childhood shaped by cognitive dissociation from abuse, posing the question of what relationship can an adult have with their abusive parent. Acceptance by Emi Nietfeld This bildungsroman memoir follows an “e” structure: The book begins with Nietfeld dreading telling her mother that she is engaged, follows the journey of her traumatic childhood of abuse and neglect, then reconnects at the starting point of the “e” by telling of the engagement, then details her low and no contact with her parents. Nietfeld’s background as a journalist and speaker informs the craft of her book in its approach of addressing both the intimate (her own experiences) and the epic (systematic abuse of children in foster care, classism, racism, poverty, and homelessness). Acceptance rejects the hero’s journey, although Nietfeld’s journey is one which portrays conventional success: graduating from Harvard and landing a high profile tech job, she reflects on how one need not be successful in order to be worthy of help. Emotionally evocative scenes restructure society’s concept of what resilience and success truly mean. Made in China by Anna Qu Anna Qu’s debut memoir follows a coming of age journey of her experience being abused and neglected at home, reporting her mother to Child Protective Services for forcing her to be a sweat factory worker as a child, and then her journey through college and unhealthy work environments as she navigates estrangement. This book is set in New York City, Wenzhou, and Xi’an. The publication of Made in China swiveled Qu’s low contact with her mother into one of complete estrangement. At the Los Angeles AWP, Qu spoke on a panel about how estrangement was the best outcome from the book, and she’s now working on an essay collection about estrangement. Books are living creatures and their impact is often outside of the control of their author’s hands. In this case, the love and labor of the book amounted to better safety of the estranged author. How to be Unmothered by Camille U Adams This lyric memoir was a finalist for the Restless Books Prize for New Immigrant Writing. The perspective of the child’s voice is written in parallel with the adult voice as narrator. This exquisite blending of narrative voices on the same page reckons with the compassion for a child experiencing abuse alongside an adult narrator holding an abusive parent accountable. The memoir grapples with how unmothering is a choice an abusive and neglectful parent makes, so that estrangement becomes necessary for the child’s survival. Adams explores multiple names to demonstrate the emotional distance to one’s estranged mother: not-mother, my mother, unmothered, Mummy, this-mother, a mother, this woman, and Soucouyant. The prose refuses to pander to the white gaze by instead rooting colloquialisms, staccato sentences, humorous rhyming, exclusion of quotation marks in dialogue, and by weaving Trinidadian oral storytelling traditions. The audiobook , recorded by Adams herself, is just as captivating. The Body Papers by Grace Talusan This winner of The Restless Books Prize for New Immigrant Writing covers an expansive amount of time from the author’s young childhood surviving abuse, deliberating in her 30s to undergo surgeries, becoming married, and participating in a Fulbright fellowship in the Philippines. All this information is mapped out in the blurb. The book includes scans of photographs, letters, and migration paperwork. Estrangement is not a main theme; a complete cutting off occupies only a few pages. This book is a testament to how family bonds can be strengthened when abusers are held accountable. Although Talusan waited until most of the elders in her family had passed before writing and sharing these memories, she felt compelled to write this book after she became an aunt and held her niece for the first time: “I realized how dangerous it was to protect the wrong people by telling only the happy stories.” Saving Five by Amanda Nguyen Astronaut and advocate Amanda Nguyen’s bestseller employs a braided structure: 1, the aftermath of rape at Harvard and having to extend her anonymous rape kit every six months, then choosing between her career and justice; and 2, the mystical journey of her multiple selves at ages 5, 15, 22, and 30 as they seek answers via memories. The way survivors tell narratives is an act of agency. Estrangement wasn’t a primary focus; instead it provided enough context to understand the further isolation in how one who is abused once is more likely to be abused, or assaulted, again. Although the majority of the book grapples with the way that rape and assault victims are responsible for the crime committed on their body, there are brief references of Nguyen’s parental estrangement scattered throughout the book and how she could never return home, as what happened at home was far worse. I’m Glad My Mom Died by Jennette McCurdy The moment I saw this controversial title for the first time, I immediately understood that the author must be a survivor of childhood abuse. McCurdy crafts this memoir by stitching together brief chapters (most chapters typically range one to five pages long). The voice remains within the perspective of the narrator’s age as she grows up; this faithfully represents the lived experience of how a child can internalize blame in order to appease an abusive and enmeshed mother.
